canberra.title: ‘Half-baked’: Timing of $4 million budget hit to ACT colleges under fire
canberra.snippet: The ACT’s secondary colleges will take a $4 million hit to their budgets for 2027 as part of a funding shake-up to make the public ...
canberra.content:
Education Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith says school budget reform was always coming. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

The ACT’s secondary colleges will take a $4 million hit to their budgets for 2027 as part of a funding shake-up to make the public school system more equitable.

The move is being driven by the School Resourcing Review, which identified a funding imbalance across the system that favoured the colleges.

But college principals, who already had to have their budgets and staffing arrangements in order by the end of June, have been caught off guard by the move to reallocate resources to schools based on need, particularly primary schools.

The Australian Education Union said the directorate should have been more transparent, calling the funding move and a shift to more teacher mobility across the system “half-baked”.

ACT branch president Angela Burroughs acknowledged the inequity in the system and the need to deploy teachers where they were most needed, but this was something that should have been done in June.

“To leave it now is incredibly late, incredibly disruptive, and will create a lot of anxiety among staff,” she said.

“Our fear is that we will lose teachers over it.”

Ms Burroughs said the government still had to review the key funding tool, the School Resourcing Allocation, which would create the major readjustment required.

She said there was concern among principals that the change would be “half-baked” as “the principals I’ve spoken to don’t have confidence that even the budget that they have been given today is going to be where they settle”.

Ms Burroughs said principals would be forced to make deep cuts to manage.

AEU ACT branch president Angela Burroughs says colleges face deep cuts. Photo: AEU.

The Education Directorate has confirmed the $4 million cut but would not say which of the nine colleges would lose funding. It has only said that six colleges will have funding within the “normal” plus or minus 5 per cent variance. Two will actually have increased funding of more than 5 per cent, while one will lose more than 5 per cent, which the union said would be about $500,000.

Ms Stephen-Smith said overall public school funding had been boosted by 7.3 per cent since 2025-26.

As a whole, 43 schools have funding within the plus-or-minus 5 per cent variance, 31 will enjoy more than a 5 per cent increase, and 18 will lose more than 5 per cent.

Ms Stephen-Smith said the goal was to achieve a fairer funding mix across ACT schools that met the needs of all students.

“The School Resourcing Review clearly indicated that that is not currently the case,” she said.

An extra pool of funding was available to support schools that would struggle to adjust.

Ms Stephen-Smith said individual schools were not being named because the budgets announced were indicative and there was room for negotiation.

“There is time for principals and school communities to work with the Education Directorate around what the impacts of some of that will look like and how they mitigate those impacts, how they work through any requirements around mobility for teachers and other school staff,” she said.

Asked about the timing of the new budgets, Ms Stephen-Smith said there would always be a day when schools received their individual budgets, based on principles that had been well understood and discussed at a high level with unions, principals, school communities and parents.

“But there’s always going to come a day when those principles translate into an actual number, and some people are going to be a bit surprised about that,” she said.

“Maybe that reflects the fact that what was not transparent previously was the inequity in some of the funding that had previously been available to schools, and that some of those adjustments weren’t quite clear to some members of the school communities.”

Education Director-General Jo Wood told Region that, in general, principals backed the direction of the reforms.

“We have principals in the schools that have the bigger challenges, the lower SES [socio-economic] schools, who really see the need,” she said.

“We have principals who might not be in those schools right now, but have been in those schools, who keep telling us this is the right direction.”

Ms Wood said the directorate would be talking to college principals about the implications of a funding decrease.

“They’re the conversations we’ll have to have,” she said.

“We don’t know what the colleges’ plans will be yet, so they will need to look at things like class sizes, and their breadth of offering.”

Ms Wood said the review also recommended more staff mobility across the system.

She said it was not just about having staff, but about having staff in the right places: “Getting some of our most experienced and high-performing staff into the schools that really need them”.

“We’re looking at how that can be improved this year, as well as what that might look like in the longer term,” Ms Wood said.

Canberra Liberals education spokesperson Elizabeth Lee said the government must explain the budget decisions.

“Will schools be forced to delay maintenance, reduce programs, or cut teaching staff and support? These are the questions staff, parents and school communities deserve answers to,” she said.

“Imposing budget reductions without proper consultation risks undermining principals’ ability to lead. The government must provide certainty about how these cuts will affect individual schools and whether students will ultimately bear the cost.”

Ms Lee said the priority should be strengthening schools, not asking them to do more with less.

canberra.title: Edge Early Learning enters voluntary administration a month after Canberra centre closure
canberra.snippet: Just over a month after one of its Canberra centres was temporarily shut following a serious medical incident involving a child, Edge Ear...
canberra.content:
Edge Early Learning has entered voluntary administration; KordaMentha has been appointed as administrator. Photo: Edge Early Learning.

Just over a month after one of its Canberra centres was temporarily shut following a serious medical incident involving a child, Edge Early Learning has entered voluntary administration.

The childcare provider, which operates multiple centres across the ACT, Queensland and South Australia, appointed KordaMentha as voluntary administrators on Tuesday (26 August).

For families, however, there is no immediate change. Edge says its centres will remain open, with children continuing to attend as usual while administrators urgently assess the company’s financial position and options for its future.

Edge operates 42 services in Queensland, 21 in SA and 3 in the ACT.

In a letter to families, Edge acknowledged the latest development could worry parents and carers.

“We understand that this news may cause concern, and we want to reassure you that our immediate priority is to ensure the ongoing operation of all centres with as little disruption as possible to children, families and educators,” it said in the statement accessed by Region.

KordaMentha’s David Johnstone, Stacey Clisby and Craig Shepard have been appointed voluntary administrators and are working with management, employees and other stakeholders while they assess the business.

Mr Johnstone confirmed that centres would continue to operate normally in the meantime.

“The care, safety and wellbeing of children remain the highest priority throughout the administration process,” the administrators said.

The development follows a difficult period for the provider.

In July, one of its Canberra centres was temporarily closed and a staff member was terminated over the handling of a serious medical incident involving a child.

A CECA spokesperson said the regulatory authorities in Queensland, South Australia, the ACT and the Australian Government are closely monitoring the issues arising with Edge Early Learning.

On 20 August 2026, following a review of a decision to impose conditions, CECA issued Edge with a notice of a three-month suspension of Edge Charnwood from operating, commencing on 3 September 2026.

Edge has the right to appeal the decision and is legally required to notify families of the suspension. Under administration, the administrator can also exercise the right to appeal.

“Families are encouraged to utilise StartingBlocks for education and care services, including ratings, regulatory visits and compliance history,” a spokesperson told Region.

The centre said families have been told there will be no change to opening hours, staffing arrangements, fees or payment dates at this stage. Child Care Subsidy entitlements will also continue, subject to normal eligibility requirements.

Edge has also assured parents that children’s day-to-day care and safety arrangements will not change, with centres continuing to operate under existing early childhood education and care regulations.

The administrators have not yet detailed the circumstances behind the company’s financial difficulties or what options are being considered for its future.

Further updates are expected once KordaMentha completes its initial assessment of the group’s financial position and possible next steps.

canberra.title: Financial crime fighting agency being criminally used to scam the public
canberra.snippet: Australia’s anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing regulator is being impersonated at an alarming rate, prompting the agen...
canberra.content:
Criminals are impersonating Austrac and Austrac officials to scam the public. Photo: Iconiq Visuals.

Australia’s anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing regulator is being impersonated at an alarming rate, prompting the agency to issue a public warning.

The Australian Transaction Reports and Analysis Centre (Austrac), which is also a specialist financial intelligence unit, is urging the public to be vigilant after discovering cases in which scammers impersonated the agency and its staff to steal money and sensitive information.

Recent cases have involved criminals impersonating Austrac investigators and senior staff, including the agency’s chief executive officer, to scam people out of significant amounts of money.

Once a rapport is built between an online scammer and an unaware member of the public, the conversation often turns to cryptocurrencies and encrypted messaging apps.

An anonymised snapshot of a real-life scam attempt. Image: Austrac.

The agency’s actual CEO, Brendan Thomas, said scammers are using emails, phone calls and messages that appear legitimate to pressure victims into making urgent payments or disclosing personal details.

“Austrac does not contact members of the public unexpectedly demanding payment,” he said.

“We take payment from reporting businesses for things like levies and infringement notices, but we are never going to ask you to pay in virtual or cryptocurrencies or through social media apps, like WhatsApp or Telegram.”

Austrac-regulated businesses may receive valid invoices from Austrac, but any unexpected request for money, personal information or urgent action claiming to be from Austrac should be treated with caution and verified through official Austrac channels before any payment is made.

As the agency’s role in protecting Australia from financial crimes becomes more visible, scammers see an opportunity to use the agency’s name, authority and reputation to deceive the public.

“Impersonation scams are getting more and more convincing, and they are designed to exploit trust in government agencies,” Mr Thomas said.

“Our public profile has grown and with it an uptick in scammers using our name and impersonating our staff to try and trick people into handing over money or sensitive information.

“These scams look official and often come with a false sense of urgency to pressure victims into acting quickly. That’s why it’s important to know what legitimate contact from Austrac actually looks like.

“Scammers don’t just steal your money; they steal your trust. They rely on fear and urgency to override your instincts, so taking a moment to pause and verify contact can prevent significant financial loss.

“If you receive a message claiming to be from Austrac and something doesn’t feel right, stop, don’t click any links and contact us using the contact details on our website.”

One recent, real-life example involved a scammer reaching out as a known Austrac contact following a consumer complaint about lost funds.

Initially, it looked helpful, and “even credible”. But it wasn’t.

The scammer first engaged in normal conversation to build trust. They claimed to have access to an Austrac investigator, and shared a real staff member’s name and LinkedIn-style profile.

The scammer then asked the victim to move the conversation to WhatsApp and promised to help recover their funds quickly.

The agency points out that this is a common tactic used by scammers.

By creating a sense of trust and urgency, they seek to move conversations onto private channels where they can request personal information or money.

Austrac does not recover lost investment funds on behalf of consumers, and will not ask people to communicate through messaging apps such as WhatsApp to resolve a matter.

Scammers are impersonating AUSTRAC personnel. Image: Austrac.

Another real-life example involved a scammer contacting a member of the public pretending to put the person in touch with Austrac’s General Counsel.

The scammer took publicly available information and added it into a message.

Austrac works closely with law enforcement, regulators and industry partners to identify and disrupt scams, but it says community awareness remains a critical line of defence.

“An Austrac staff member will never ask you to make an additional payment to engage with AUSTRAC, whether that relates to a complaint you’ve made, or a matter Austrac is addressing with you,” its warning statement says.

“In almost all cases, Austrac will contact you before taking any action and explain what is happening.

“If you need to make a payment to Austrac, we will notify you in writing and give you time to contact us if you have any questions or concerns.”

canberra.title: A review is on the way but committee wants its own inquiry into Secure Local Jobs Code
canberra.snippet: The contentious Secure Local Jobs Code will face a new inquiry despite the ACT Government preparing for a review as recommended by a comm...
canberra.content:
26 August 2026

Join the conversation

2

Canberra Liberals leader Mark Parton wants the Secure Local Jobs Code scrapped. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

The contentious Secure Local Jobs Code will face a new inquiry despite the ACT Government preparing for a review as recommended by a committee inquiry in June.

The Standing Committee on Public Accounts and Administration announced on Tuesday (25 August) that it would undertake its own inquiry into the effectiveness and operation of the code, which Canberra Liberals Leader Mark Parton wants scrapped.

The Liberal committee chair James Milligan said the inquiry would examine whether the code was achieving its objectives in terms of supporting local jobs, upholding industrial relations standards and delivering value for money.

According to the terms of reference, the committee will look at its effectiveness in supporting local jobs including subcontractors and apprentices, small and medium sized enterprises, including in supply chains and the not-for-profit sector.

The code has been frequently criticised for favouring larger businesses and union influence.

The new inquiry will look at another criticism, that the administrative and compliance burden on tenderers is too onerous and imposes barriers to participation.

Union membership of the Secure Local Jobs Advisory Council will also come under scrutiny when the committee examines the appropriateness of the council’s role, composition and operation.

The announcement comes a day after Mr Parton repeated calls for the code to be scrapped in relation to the disruption to the light rail project because of a lapsed certificate.

The Opposition Leader has ramped up his calls since the release of the ACT Integrity Commission’s Operation Kingfisher report into the Campbell School upgrade.

He is demanding the government immediately abolish the code, terminate the UnionsACT Memorandum of Understanding that grants privileged access to procurement information and tenderer details, scrap the 2023 Ethical Treatment of Workers Evaluation Direction that embeds union influence over live procurements and mandate full disclosure of any external representations seeking to influence the outcome of tenders.

The government said the code was integral to protecting workers’ rights but the Liberals said this could be achieved by enforcing workplace laws through independent regulation.

Finance Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith said the government had already started work to establish a review, including consultation with the Secure Local Jobs Advisory Council.

Ms Stephen-Smith said the government would consult with the committee on how best to manage the obvious risks of duplication between these processes.

She said that many of the issues raised by stakeholders related to the effectiveness of local industry participation policies and the management of contractors and subcontracting arrangements, rather than the operation of the code itself.

“The government’s review will include consideration of the code’s role in the wider procurement system, recognising there has been significant procurement reform in recent years,” Ms Stephen-Smith said.

“I would welcome a conversation with the committee to discuss how its inquiry can further inform the government’s work and hear a broad range of stakeholder perspectives.”

Mr Milligan said the government had not published a formal response to the earlier committee inquiry.

The Assembly or the Public Accounts and Administration Committee had not received any advice from the government about a review.

“As such, this Committee decided to conduct its own inquiry,” Mr Milligan said.

The committee is calling for stakeholders from the construction, cleaning, security and traffic management industries as well as community and nonprofit groups to make a submission.

Submissions close on Tuesday 6 October.

canberra.title: Having filmed dingos for David Attenborough, this Canberra cinematographer is unveiling his next project
canberra.snippet: For nearly a decade, Daniel Hunter has been filming dingos and showcasing them to the world through programs like Sir David Attenborough’...
canberra.content:
Canberra cinematographer Daniel Hunter has been filming dingos for nearly a decade, with his work featuring in some of the biggest wildlife documentaries ever. Photo: Daniel Hunter.

For nearly a decade, Daniel Hunter has been filming dingos and showcasing them to the world through programs like Sir David Attenborough’s Seven Worlds, One Planet.

Mr Hunter has observed the vital role that dingos play in Australia’s ecosystem, including controlling invasive species and reducing overgrazing in Namadgi National Park.

“I completed my PhD focusing on dingos in the Greater Blue Mountains area. I studied them closely for about four years and gained a pretty good understanding of them and how they existed in the environment,” Mr Hunter said.

“At the same time, I was really pursuing a filmmaking career. I had filmed a few things with dingos, but then around 2018, the BBC reached out and asked if I could do some filming for a David Attenborough documentary series.”

Mr Hunter worked with the BBC for several months to film the dingos back in 2018, resulting in footage that had never been captured before.

“We basically spent a month trying to figure out how to film them out at Namadgi National Park, which was very cool because they really hadn’t been filmed professionally out there at all, and they certainly hadn’t been filmed hunting kangaroos.

“We were able to get the very first footage of them hunting kangaroos in the wild, naturally, which was awesome. Ever since, I’ve been heading to the National Park about twice a year to go film.”

Mr Hunter’s footage of the dingos can be seen on episode four of Seven Worlds, One Planet (2019).

One of Mr Hunter’s images illustrated by artist Lillian Webb. Photo: Supplied.

Since first filming dingos, Mr Hunter said he has learnt more than he could have imagined, but it’s the animals’ appearance that has shocked him the most.

“I think the biggest surprise, when I tell people what I’ve been doing and show them the footage, is when people see that a lot of white dingos and black dingos are right on Canberra’s doorstep,” he said.

“For me, it’s been really cool to be able to study the family units over a really long period of time and watch how family-committed they are.

“As siblings, they really support one another, and it’s quite special to see that interaction play out.”

Now, the cinematographer and biologist is taking what he has learnt about Australia’s iconic native dog and is teaming up with wildlife illustrators, Field Edition, to share just how special dingos are with a new audience.

“I’ve partnered with a really talented natural history illustrator. Her name’s Lillian Webb, and she’s based in Newcastle.

“I’ve basically used some of the photos and videos that I’ve captured over the last sort of 10 years, and given some of those images to her to basically create a natural history plate, similar to artworks used by the first European colonisers when they arrived in Australia.

” I’ve used a white dingo as the sort of main feature, but a lot of people aren’t aware that dingos come in all different colours, and they’re completely purebred, even if they’re white or black or anything in between.

“I’m really proud of this project with Lillian, and we’re really excited for people to see some of the works.”

Field Editions artworks can be seen and purchased here.

australia.title: Productivity Commission says ‘line was crossed’ when WA premier labelled them ‘east coast clowns’ over GST
australia.snippet: Commissioner Angela Jackson also said it was ‘disappointing’ that Anthony Albanese had ruled out changes to Western Australia’s GST arran...
australia.content:
The Productivity Commission has condemned attacks on its integrity as “unacceptable” after its scathing assessment of Western Australia’s sweetheart GST deal as a costly mistake sparked a fierce political backlash and name-calling.

Angela Jackson, a productivity commissioner and co-author of the report, said the country’s leading independent economic advisory body welcomed criticism and comments on its work.

But Jackson said comments from Roger Cook, the Western Australian premier, lampooning the commission as “east coast clowns” and describing the report as deceitful had “crossed a line”.

Cook said in a statement: “I’m doing exactly what I’ll always do and putting WA first” and that “it is important we continue to present our economic arguments”.

“To the Productivity Commission it may be academic but for Western Australians it’s our lives, and I’ll fight for every dollar.”

As Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, defended the “good people” at the commission and chided the WA Labor leader for his “inappropriate” language, Jackson said “we are used to public debate”.

“In fact, we welcome it at the Productivity Commission, it’s why we have interim reports,” she told ABC radio before a meeting of national cabinet on Wednesday afternoon.

“We are aiming, of course, to inform public policy debate, which can often get heated. Our view is that a line was crossed in terms of the nature of those comments from the Western Australian premier.”

Jackson linked the tone of the criticism and the language used “to attack our integrity” with “something that more broadly we are seeing in public debate internationally”.

“We want to call this out as being unacceptable.”

When asked about Cook’s sledge, Chalmers told journalists on Wednesday: “I don’t believe that is appropriate.”

“I think you can disagree with the conclusions of the Productivity Commission without denigrating them. I think it’s important that even when those conclusions are contested, as they often will be, that we continue to respect the people of the PC and the really important work that they do.”

The commission was asked to review the 2018 legislation put in place under the Morrison government.

That deal fundamentally changed the way the commonwealth distributed the GST pool between the states and territories.

The commission’s interim report found that the 2018 legislation had achieved none of its objectives, made the system less fair and had funnelled an extra $23bn in taxpayer money to the nation’s richest state.

The interim recommendation to reverse the deal was backed by all other states and territories, but was immediately declared dead in the water by Anthony Albanese.

“What I believe is, very clearly, there will be no change to WA GST arrangements whilst I’m prime minister,” Albanese said on Monday.

Jackson said Albanese’s comments were “disappointing at this point in the process”.

The PC will now do further consultation before a final report due by the end of this year.

“It’s important for us to indicate that that process will not be influenced by the prime minister’s comments, that we are above politics,” Jackson said.

“And that’s a very important position that we hold within the public policy landscape in Australia.”

Independent MP Allegra Spender said it was “frustrating” that Albanese had effectively ruled out any changes to WA’s GST deal before the independent inquiry had run its course.

“When Roger Cook calls highly qualified and capable public servants ‘clowns’ he is seeking to disparage people tasked with giving government frank advice,” Spender said.

“You may disagree with their views, but this kind of language directed at public servants is simply unacceptable from major public figures.”

She added that it was also “disappointing to hear the federal resources minister [Madeleine King] describe these comments as ‘fair enough’ on radio yesterday”.

On Wednesday, the industry and science minister, Tim Ayres, said there were “strong views” about the GST issue in WA, and a “colourful contest” about the issue when asked about Cook’s comments.

“The Productivity Commission has important work to do for Australia and we’re not a government that gets reports that contest our view and has a glass jaw about that,” Ayres told the ABC.

Ayres claimed WA was a state with “particular needs” and defended Albanese ruling out any GST changes even before the PC’s final report.

“[Albanese] gets Western Australia, understands what Western Australians need and the contribution that they make. And everything he’s done has been completely consistent with that view and it should have surprised nobody.”

Cook’s office has been approached for comment.

australia.title: Australia news live: PM, premiers and chief ministers sign firearms agreement; Sarah Hanson-Young scathing on Malcolm Roberts’ gay rights comments
australia.snippet: Follow updates live Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Angela Jackson, the commissioner of the Productivity Com...
australia.content:
National cabinet agrees to tighten gun laws

Tom McIlroy

State and territory leaders and the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, have agreed to further tighten national gun laws in a meeting in Sydney.

Albanese said federal government intelligence would be shared with state and territory law enforcement agencies as part of the deal, and that only Australian citizens would be allowed to hold gun licences.

The push comes after the deaths in December’s antisemitic shooting at Bondi Beach and as the federal government’s national buyback plan falters due to low take-up by the states. Only NSW and the ACT have signed up so far.

Albanese said 3D printed gun technology would be banned, along with sharing of materials about their production.

Key events

  • 50m ago

    National cabinet agrees to tighten gun laws

  • 1h ago

    National cabinet front media after conclusion of today’s meeting

  • 3h ago

    Major childcare provider Edge Early Learning goes into voluntary administration

  • 3h ago

    Chalmers defends ‘good people’ of the PC from WA premier’s sledges

  • 4h ago

    NSW police investigating after alleged theft of $350,000 in oysters

  • 5h ago

  • 8h ago

  • 8h ago

  • 10h ago

    Greens say national cabinet needs to refocus on gendered violence ‘before it’s too late’

  • 11h ago

    Man charged after allegedly stabbing woman with scissors

  • 11h ago

    Good morning

Patrick Commins

Roger Cook brushes off criticism of ‘east coast clowns’ sledge

Roger Cook, the West Australian premier, has not apologised for referring to Productivity Commission officials as “east coast clowns”, saying “I’m doing exactly what I’ll always do and putting WA first”.

The Productivity Commission’s review process is not over yet, so it is important we continue to present our economic arguments.

Cook has come under fire for his sledge, triggered by the PC’s interim report last week which described the Morrison government’s sweetheart GST deal with WA as a costly mistake that should be reversed.

Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, this afternoon backed his top independent economic advisory body, saying the WA Labor leader’s insult was inappropriate.

Independent MP Allegra Spender described Cook’s name-calling as “simply unacceptable”.

But Cook was defiant, in a statement saying that “to the Productivity Commission it may be academic but for Western Australians it’s our lives, and I’ll fight for every dollar”.

Cook said he was advised that a meeting between his treasurer, Rita Saffioti, and PC officials on Wednesday to discuss the inquiry was “positive, polite and robust”. He said:

One thing the Productivity Commission’s report didn’t do is acknowledge Western Australia’s massive contribution to the national economy. They also didn’t explain why this report is so different to their 2018 report.

Victorian legal advocates oppose potential new police powers to allow officers access to people’s financial records without warrant

The Federation of Community Legal Centres says it is “deeply concerned” about proposed police powers that would allow officers to access a person’s financial records without a judge-issued warrant.

The proposed powers, which would apply to all offences, are part of upper-house amendments to crime reforms that have passed Victoria’s lower house.

The chief executive, Louisa Gibbs, described the changes as “frightening” and raised serious privacy concerns.

The proposed powers will allow police to authorise themselves to obtain information without notifying the person who holds the bank account and without a warrant.

The process of independent judicial consideration before granting police a warrant is an important check that our community expects and deserves.

Removing this step presents an unacceptable risk to the rights of all Victorians, and this amendment should be immediately withdrawn.

‘It is hard to imagine a world without her’: Albanese pays tribute to Dolly Parton during national cabinet media address

Continuing on that Sydney press conference, the prime minister has taken a moment to pay tribute to the late Dolly Parton. He said:

Dolly Parton made our world a better place in so many ways. It is hard to imagine a world without her. A singer and songwriter of rare power and talent, she also shone brightly as an actor, an author and a philanthropist who made such a contribution to promoting education around the world, as well as funding hospitals and making an enormous difference.

She had such an extraordinarily large personality and was much loved here in Australia and around the world … there will be a lot of broken hearts in Australia today and may I just say that Dolly Parton, I’m sure will rest in peace.

She lived loudly and she lived a great life. She will be much missed.

National cabinet agrees to tighten gun laws

Tom McIlroy

State and territory leaders and the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, have agreed to further tighten national gun laws in a meeting in Sydney.

Albanese said federal government intelligence would be shared with state and territory law enforcement agencies as part of the deal, and that only Australian citizens would be allowed to hold gun licences.

The push comes after the deaths in December’s antisemitic shooting at Bondi Beach and as the federal government’s national buyback plan falters due to low take-up by the states. Only NSW and the ACT have signed up so far.

Albanese said 3D printed gun technology would be banned, along with sharing of materials about their production.

National cabinet front media after conclusion of today’s meeting

The prime minister, premiers and chief ministers have just held a press conference in Sydney after today’s national cabinet meeting.

Anthony Albanese outlined the key items they discussed:

  • Working together to form new artificial intelligence laws that he says will be legislated next year. They will also ensure power prices are protected and datacentres are located in the right places;

  • Accelerating policies to end gender-based violence;

  • Signing a new firearms agreement, aimed at improving laws after the Bondi massacre;

  • An additional $125m will be committed as part of the fight against bird flu;

  • Fuel security will continue to be monitored as the conflict in the Middle East reaches its six-month mark this week

Albanese described the meeting as “an excellent meeting” and thanked the panel for their “constructive engagement”.

Cait Kelly

Family violence advocates call for government’s commitment to action after national cabinet

The No to Violence chief executive, Phillip Ripper, has called on the national cabinet to commit to tangible action that prevents violence, intervenes earlier and holds men who use violence accountable.

He said:

Consultation on the next National Action Plan has reinforced a clear message to governments: more of the same will not deliver the change Australia needs. While we must keep doing everything possible to keep women and children safe, we will never see the dial shift until we tackle the problem at the source.

Australia spends billions of dollars every year responding to the consequences of men’s use of family violence, while police and courts across the country remain under enormous pressure. Yet comparatively little is invested in prevention, early intervention, holding men accountable for their behaviour, and providing effective pathways away from violence.

Achol Arok

With Nick Visser off, I’ll be here to guide you through the rest of the afternoon’s news!

Teenage girl spared prison in first ‘adult time’ sentence

The first child to be sentenced under Victoria’s “adult time for violent crime” laws has been spared jail for a brazen and violent aggravated carjacking.

The 16-year-old girl, who cannot be named, was instead sentenced to an 18-month youth justice supervision order for the 27 February incident.

The teenager admitted she threatened a taxi driver with a knife before stealing his car about two hours after the “adult time” legislation came into effect.

Under the changes, children aged 14 and older who commit home invasions or aggravated carjackings must face the county court, where penalties are tougher than a children’s court.

Victorian county court judge Scott Johns found the offending was “brazen and violent”.

But her upbringing and the absence of any criminal record meant she should be sentenced under the Children’s Act.

The judge said on Wednesday:

Specific deterrence and protection of the community would be best served by your rehabilitation in the community.

No doubt for many cases of aggravated carjacking, sentences imposed under the (adult) Sentencing Act will be necessary.

I’ve concluded your case is not one of them.

He noted it was her first time before the courts and she had a difficult upbringing, having been in and out of child protection and residential care since the age of two.

– AAP

Tory Shepherd

Sarah Hanson-Young condemns Malcolm Roberts’s comments about gay rights

Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young had a scathing take on One Nation MP Malcolm Roberts being “in two minds” about gay rights.

Roberts made the comments when he was questioned about the party’s director, James Ashby.

Hanson-Young said this afternoon it “should be absolutely obvious” that LGBTQ+ Australians are indeed equal:

No one should be in two minds about that … that every Australian is equal. And I question Malcolm Roberts. He says he’s in two minds about this. Well, I wonder whether he’s even got one.

Major childcare provider Edge Early Learning goes into voluntary administration

Edge Early Learning, a major childcare provider with centres in Queensland, South Australia and the ACT, has gone into voluntary administration.

The company will continue to operate all centres on a “business-as-usual basis’ with no change to care arrangements or opening hours and staffing.

The company said on its website:

We understand that this may be a confusing and stressful development for families who rely upon Edge Early Learning to provide care for their children.

Jordyn Beazley

Hi there, I’ll now be with you for the next little while.

Nick Visser

That’s all for me. Jordyn Beazley will take things from here. Take care.

Benita Kolovos

Jess Wilson says secret levy to help fund Suburban Rail Loop is ‘the final nail in the coffin’ for Victorian government

The Victorian opposition leader, Jess Wilson, has described the revelation public transport users have been paying a secret levy to help fund the Suburban Rail Loop as “the final nail in the coffin for this government”.

An auditor general report into the first stage of the SRL – from Cheltenham to Box Hill – tabled in parliament this morning, revealed the government added a 1% levy on public transport fares on 1 January 2025 but did not inform Victorians.

The auditor general said 60% of the revenue earned will go to SRL East.

The premier, Ben Carroll, was public transport minister when the levy was approved in 2021.

Speaking outside parliament this afternoon, Wilson said:

When VAGO handed down this report today, I expected to see cost blowouts. I expected to see delays to this project, but never in my wildest dreams did I think that there would be secret taxes levied on Victorians.

She said Carroll has “lied to Victorians” – and questioned “How many more secret taxes are there?”

Wilson went on:

This is just the final nail in the coffin for this government. I think we’ve seen a government that will lie to Victorians time and time and time again but hiding this, and for the auditor general to expose it, for the premier to fail to be upfront with Victorians at any point in time when he signed off on this, when he went to the 2022 election, when he became the premier of this state, it just demonstrates Ben Carroll has no integrity.

australia.title: Suburban Rail Loop: Victorian government secretly increased public transport fares to help pay for controversial SRL
australia.snippet: Labor put ‘levy on all public transport fares in metropolitan Melbourne and regional Victoria’ since January 2025, auditor general finds,...
australia.content:
Questions have been raised about Ben Carroll’s knowledge of a “secret tax” the Victorian government has slapped on public transport fares to help pay for the Suburban Rail Loop and other Big Build projects.

The existence of the levy was revealed in an auditor general report tabled in parliament on Wednesday, which also threw doubt on whether the first stage of the multibillion-dollar project – a 26km stretch of twin tunnels from Cheltenham to Box Hill dubbed SRL East – can be delivered on time or within budget.

In place since 1 January 2025, the levy involves a 1% annual increase on all public transport fares in metropolitan Melbourne and regional Victoria, on top of existing adjustments in line with inflation.

According to information provided to the auditor general by the Department of Treasury and Finance (DTF), it will be in place until 2062, when daily full fare in zone 1 and 2 would have risen to $39.20.

“The government plans to allocate 60% of the revenue it collects through the levy, estimated at $4.8bn in net present value (NPV) terms to 2062, to fund SRL East,” the report reads.

The auditor general said the levy will be SRL East’s “largest source of value capture revenue” but it was not made public.

“The government and Transport Victoria did not acknowledge the levy in their public communications about the 2025 and 2026 annual fare increases. As at June 2026, they still have not announced it,” the report reads.

Instead, the government held a press conference in December 2025 to announce that $11.5bn in revenue for the project would be raised through five other value capture measures: using existing land tax and windfall gains tax revenue in SRL East precincts, infrastructure contributions from property developers, revenue from state-initiated property development and a car parking levy.

The opposition leader, Jess Wilson, described the levy as a “secret public transport tax” and a “scandal of the highest order”.

“When VAGO handed down this report today, I expected to see cost blowouts. I expected to see delays to this project, but never in my wildest dreams did I think that there would be secret taxes levied on Victorians,” she told reporters.

Wilson blamed the new premier, Ben Carroll, who was public transport minister at the time the levy was approved in 2021.

“Ben Carroll signed off on this tax, went to an election refusing to tell Victorians about it, and has stood up every single day since saying that he has integrity when it’s very clear he does not have an ounce of it,” she said.

The Greens leader Ellen Sandell said the affair proved why “trust in the major parties is collapsing”.

“Victorians were never told they were being hit with a secret levy to fund Labor’s Big Build, which has been shrouded in secrecy from the start,” she said. “The stench around Labor is becoming impossible to hide.”

Senior government sources have sought to distance Carroll from the decision, saying the policy was approved at meeting of the state’s four-person budget and finance committee in December 2023, when he was not a member. At the time, members included the former premier Jacinta Allan, the former treasurer Tim Pallas and ministers Danny Pearson and Jaclyn Symes.

The auditor general report notes the government “first approved the levy in August 2021”. At the time, Carroll was public transport minister.

It said the levy was also confirmed by government in “December 2023 and November 2024 when it made further decisions on the project’s value capture revenue package”. Carroll had been added to the committee in 2024.

Carroll, who became premier last month, issued a statement in response to the report saying he would “lead a government that levels with Victorians”.

“I’m a premier taking the state in a new direction and Victorians deserve to know what their money is buying. Under my leadership, they will,” he said.

“When costs change, we’ll tell you. When we find savings, we’ll bank them.”

The report notes the levy has generated $6.2m between January 2025 and the end of February 2026, “significantly” less revenue than forecast. This is due to policies such as making public transport free for children and free for seniors on weekends, free travel during the fuel crisis and half-price fares until the end of the year.

The auditor general also revealed the state government has approved budget funding of $23.3bn for the project but only publicly announced $11.8bn.

A funding gap of $5.5bn also remains because the federal government has committed “less to the project than has been assumed and requested by the state”.

The gap means the state “does not have sufficient funding approved to sign the contract for the second stations package”, the report said, which is contributing to “significant delays” putting at risk SRL East’s promised 2035 completion date.

It said the project is “more likely than not to exceed its publicly disclosed cost of up to $34.5bn”, due to costs related to “unexpected ground conditions and contamination”, “higher than expected market pricing” for the linewide and station contracts, and “added project costs and delays because of government decisions to slow down spending on the project to manage the state’s debt levels”.

The report comes a day after Carroll pledged to deliver $2bn in savings for SRL East.

australia.title: Afternoon Update: Woolworths explains profit surge amid cost-of-living crisis; fears for famous seal; and Dolly Parton’s life in quotes
australia.snippet: Want to get this in your inbox every weekday? Sign up for the Afternoon Update here , and start your day with our Morning Mail newsletter...
australia.content:
Good afternoon.

Woolworths has reported a $175m surge in net profit to $1.14bn, but the supermarket giant’s chief executive, Amanda Bardwell, said it had not done so by lifting shelf prices.

The supermarket duopoly, Woolworths and Coles, has previously faced criticism for fattening profit margins during periods of high living costs at the expense of higher prices for shoppers.

Woolworths pointed to the drop to “ongoing cost-of-living pressures on households” and the ever popular Ooshies campaign as the reason shoppers continued to choose the supermarket giant.

Sydney Dance Company is marking four decades since it made its home at the Wharf theatres at Walsh Bay. As part of the celebrations, the company is presenting an exhibition in the foyer of its Wharf home, developed in partnership with Museums of History NSW. With photographs, oral histories and archival material, the exhibition explores the people, stories and spaces that have shaped the company and the wharf precinct itself.

What they said …

“We’d hate to see him get the flu.” – Lynn Murrell, president of the Southwest Environment Alliance, when asked about Sammy the seal

Since H5 bird flu arrived in Portland, Victoria, the situation has been “pretty grim”, with many dead and suffering birds found on the beach. But since the first confirmed case in a fur seal on Sunday at Beachport, South Australia – a two-hour trip over the border – people have been worried for their local “pet seal”, known as Sammy.

Dolly Parton in her own words: ageing, sex appeal and motivation

The singer Dolly Parton, who has died aged 80, had a ready fund of quips, most mercilessly self-deprecating. “It takes a lot of money to look this cheap” was perhaps the most famous, and undoubtedly the one that best captured her appetite for glitz and mischief.

australia.title: Fears grow for fourth rate hike after Australia sees higher-than-expected July inflation
australia.snippet: Bureau of Statistics says CPI was 3.5% in July, casting doubt on Reserve Bank meeting its 2.5% inflation target without further hike Foll...
australia.content:
Fears are growing that the Reserve Bank will hit millions of mortgage holders with a fourth rate hike this year, after inflation eased in July but by far less than expected.

Consumer prices climbed by 3.5% through the year, down from 3.8% in the previous month, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

That compared unfavourably to the forecast 3.3% annual rate predicted by economists leading into the result.

The Reserve Bank’s preferred underlying inflation measure, which removes the most volatile prices, had been expected to moderate but instead was stuck at 3.6%.

Brendan Rynne, KPMG’s chief economist, said “today’s data supports the view that without policy action we may be in for a long, costly grind to get inflation under control”.

“The Reserve Bank may have missed an opportunity at the last board meeting to get ahead of the game by raising rates,” Rynne said.

The disappointing update comes a day after minutes from the most recent RBA meeting showed board members were unconvinced that they would be able to hit their 2.5% inflation target by the end of next year and would react to any evidence that price pressures were not easing as expected.

While the decision on 11 August to hold the cash rate at 4.35% was unanimous, a number of board members thought another hike this year was “quite possible”.

Economists, many of whom had ruled out further rate increases, said the latest ABS figures heightened the chance of a November hike, with NAB analysts declaring that their call for no further rate hikes was “under review”.

Phil O’Donaghoe, chief economist at Deutsche Bank, said he now expected the RBA would move as early as the next meeting in September, describing the underlying price growth as “intolerably high”.

“We think the July CPI [consumer price index] leaves little room for the RBA to do anything other than follow through on its hawkish posturing, and the earlier it does, the better,” O’Donaghoe said.

As expected, the end of the fuel excise relief in July helped push up pump prices by 7.5% in the month after falling for three months in a row, the ABS figures showed.

But My Bui, an economist at AMP, said “housing remains Australia’s chronic issue”, as home building costs lifted by 5.7% in the year to July, and rents by 3.6%.

Bui said she still predicted an RBA rate hike in November, but “a September hike is certainly plausible”.

The ABS said that the increase in construction costs “was driven by project home builders raising base prices to pass through higher labour and materials costs over the year”.

The price of takeaway and restaurant meal prices climbed by 4.5% through the year, driven by higher operating costs including ingredients and the increase in the minimum wage from 1 July, the ABS said.

world.title: Prince Harry quits board of wildlife charity after rangers’ human rights abuses
world.snippet: Spokesperson for Duke of Sussex says he remains an ‘active and avid supporter’ of African Parks’ mission The Duke of Sussex has stepped d...
world.content:
The Duke of Sussex has stepped down from the board of a major African wildlife charity that had been at the centre of a human rights controversy.

Prince Harry’s spokesperson confirmed he was no longer a trustee of African Parks, which admitted last year that human rights abuses were committed by its rangers in the Republic of the Congo.

The charity’s admission followed an independent review into allegations made by members of the Baka community.

In a 2024 report published by the Mail on Sunday newspaper, community members accused African Parks rangers of beating, waterboarding and raping locals to stop them from accessing their ancestral forests, which are now in a conservation area.

After the review, African Parks published a statement acknowledging that human rights abuses occurred in the Odzala-Kokoua national park, which it manages. It said that it had improved its safeguarding processes both at the park and institutionally.

A spokesperson for Harry said the duke, who was president of the charity for six years before he became a member of its board of directors in 2023, remained an active and avid supporter of African Parks.

“The duke is proud of his 10 years with African Parks and fully supports the ongoing strengthening of its board,” the spokesperson said.

“His commitment to conservation in Africa continues, and he remains a supporter of African Parks’ mission.”

Survival International, a global human rights charity that campaigns for the rights of Indigenous people, had called on Harry to step down as a member of the board.

Caroline Pearce, the executive director of Survival International, said it was “outrageous that for 10 years Prince Harry has served African Parks” while people working for it had “been responsible for abuse and violence against Indigenous people. His departure doesn’t undo that record — African Parks itself must now be held accountable, and must abandon this model of fortress conservation for good.”

Founded 26 years ago, African Parks manages more than 20m hectares (50m acres) in partnership with 13 African governments and hundreds of local communities.

African Parks expressed “deep gratitude” to the duke on concluding his tenure after his 10-year commitment to the organisation.

“His relationship with the organisation dates back to Malawi in July 2016, when he supported one of the largest elephant translocations in history. He served as president for six years before being appointed a member of the board of directors,” it said.

“Over the years, the duke has brought global attention to the urgent need for biodiversity protection for the benefit of people and wildlife, and has contributed greatly to promoting philanthropy for the cause of conservation in Africa. The duke remains deeply committed to this cause, and remains a strong supporter of African Parks’ work.”

The announcement comes as the Duke and Duchess of Sussex are due to relocate to the UK from California with their children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five.

Former Suits star Meghan is said to be pursuing an acting role, with reports she has been in talks about a role in the third series of Guy Ritchie’s Netflix hit The Gentlemen, swiftly followed by other reports that the deal was off.

The couple are understood to be planning an “extended stay” in the UK, and their children are already enrolled in school, but it has not been confirmed for how long.

world.title: Video shows hundreds held captive after Nigeria mosque kidnapping
world.snippet: Gunmen ‌attacked worshippers in Dekara village on Friday taking women, children and older people An armed group has posted a video showin...
world.content:
An armed group has posted a video showing what ⁠residents said were about ⁠600 women, children and ​older people abducted in an attack on a mosque in Nigeria’s north-central Niger State last week.

The video, posted on Facebook and WhatsApp, ⁠showed large groups of people seated in a forested area surrounded by armed men. Several children could be heard crying in the background.

Mass kidnappings for ransom have become common in ⁠parts of north-western and north-central Nigeria, where heavily armed gangs frequently raid villages, schools and highways and hold them until ​paid large sums of money. The violence was previously focused in the north of the country, but gunmen have ‌increasingly moved south.

The video surfaced two days after the latest kidnapping, when gunmen ‌attacked worshippers at the mosque in Dekara village during Friday prayers, taking people away in what residents said were simultaneous raids on several communities.

In the video, a gunman speaking in Hausa addressed families of the captives and urged them to identify relatives among the people in the footage.

“These are all your people. We are showing you this video so that you can identify your family members, your fathers, mothers, children ‌and relatives,” the gunman said.

Reuters could not verify the exact date or the location where the video was filmed. However, no older version of the video was found posted ​online before Sunday.

Four residents said they were able to confirm the identities of some of those seized.

“The people in the video are from Dekara. I’ve identified 13 people that I know,” Ibrahim Abubakar said.

Another resident, Abdulmutallib Muqaddas Dindi, said those who appeared in the video had been seized during the prayers. “We have ⁠identified our elders, relatives, and some of us have seen their wives and children ​in the video,” he said.

Police ​and state authorities did not respond ​to requests for comment on Monday. Police had earlier confirmed an attack on worshippers in ​the area but said ‌they could not ​verify the number of people ​abducted.

Jamilu Ibrahim, another resident, appealed to the federal and state authorities to secure the release of the captives, pointing out the number of mothers with infants and children among those shown in the footage.

world.title: Children make up half of suspected mpox cases in Guinea-Bissau as epidemic spreads
world.snippet: West African country reports 46 suspected cases in outbreak declared in July, amid fears virus may be spreading undetected More than half...
world.content:
More than half of the mpox cases reported in Guinea-Bissau have been among children, local authorities have said, almost two months since the country announced an epidemic.

A national outbreak was declared on 4 July, just over a week after a 27-year-old woman became the first confirmed case of mpox in the west African country. Since then, there have been seven confirmed cases and 46 suspected cases. Half of those patients have been children, with 16 under the age of four.

In a statement on Thursday, Unicef warned that because the country’s health surveillance systems were fragile, the virus is probably spreading undetected, leaving even more children at risk.

Sandra Martins, the country’s deputy representative for Unicef, said: “This is the first time mpox cases have been reported in Guinea-Bissau, making even a small outbreak a major public health event.”

Mpox is an infectious viral disease that can be transmitted through close contact. There have been more than 2,000 mpox-related deaths among tens of thousands of cases recorded across east, central and west Africa since January 2024.

Health workers say the Clade variants are consistent with viruses circulating in neighbouring countries, meaning that a risk of cross‑border transmission in the region remains strong. The vast majority of confirmed cases are in the Bissau autonomous sector, where the capital is, while one case is in the nearby Biombo area. No deaths have been reported to date.

Dr Magda Robalo, a former health minister who led the country’s Covid-19 response, said that to eliminate the “biggest gaps in the health system right now”, increased surveillance would have to be prioritised and frontline capacity reinforced.

“Even though the numbers are small, new cases have appeared intermittently over several weeks, which means transmission is ongoing,” said Robalo, who is also co-founder of the Institute for Global Health and Development and former director of communicable diseases for the World Health Organization.

The outbreak comes as the country grapples with infrastructure challenges and the aftermath of the suspension of last November’s presidential election by the military, which remains in power. There was no electricity throughout Thursday in Bissau for instance because of petrol scarcity since the weekend.

Many public health laboratories in the region lack equipment to deal with epidemics but have institutional knowledge from handling other crises.

In Guinea-Bissau, that is no different but there is also a sense of urgency, with primary schools scheduled to reopen across the country in September. After the outbreak was declared, community health workers immediately began a door-to-door public awareness campaign with megaphones and translated leaflets, supported by the health ministry and international agencies.

These grassroots initiatives are seen as vital for building public trust in the public health sector. Earlier this year, the country suspended a controversial US-funded trial on hepatitis B vaccinations for newborns, citing ethical concerns and procedural flaws. The decision was lauded by many across the continent and has highlighted sensitivities around emergency health interventions.

world.title: Landslide at waste mound in Guinea capital kills 30, government says
world.snippet: Dump site in Conakry, which minister had just promised to move, collapsed after heavy rain in west African state A ⁠landslide at a huge w...
world.content:
A ⁠landslide at a huge waste dump in Guinea’s capital has killed 30 people, the government said on Sunday, after heavy rains overnight prompted it to ⁠collapse, engulfing nearby tents and shacks.

The incident occurred less than a week after the government announced plans to close the ⁠site and relocate the waste because of the threat it posed, especially during the rainy season, which causes landslides and fatal flash ⁠floods each year in crowded, underdeveloped cities across parts of West Africa.

The landslide took ​place at about 2am (3am UK time) ‌in the Gbessia commune ‌of Conakry, according to a government statement.

The death toll was 30, with six ‌people seriously injured and 16 more lightly injured, the statement said.

Rescue workers were using excavators and other tools to clear the site of the landslide, which witnesses said was large enough to bury an apartment building along with more precarious dwellings.

One woman, Cire Diallo, told reporters at the scene that her five children were killed. “I ‌have lost all my children. All I can do is put my trust in God,” she said.

Guinea holds the world’s largest bauxite ​reserves and richest untapped iron ore deposit at Simandou, where a massive mining project was launched in November. But the west African country has poor infrastructure and widespread poverty, with 3.7 million of its 15.1 million people living on less than $4.20 a day, according to a ⁠World Bank report published in April.

On Thursday Guinea’s minister of territorial administration, Djénabou Touré Camara​, announced ​that the government was closing ​the landfill because it was unsafe and said the waste was to ​be relocated outside Conakry.

The prime ‌minister, Amadou Oury ​Bah, visited ​the landfill on Sunday to assess the damage and supervise the response, the government statement said, adding that people should “remain calm, show solidarity, and strictly follow the instructions of rescue services and the competent authorities”.

world.title: US deports 20 people to Liberia, the first of 1,200 migrants under Trump deal
world.snippet: Agreement is among largest third-country deportations driven by Trump administration’s immigration crackdown Twenty deportees from the Un...
world.content:
Twenty deportees from the United States arrived in Liberia on Thursday, as part of a new agreement that will see the west African country receive as many as 1,200 people under the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

The group arrived at the Roberts international airport outside the capital, Monrovia. The Liberia-US agreement is one of the largest third-country deportation arrangements pursued by the administration since Trump returned to office last year.

The Liberian information minister, Jerolinmek Piah said the 1,200 deportees will include African nationals as well as nationals from North America, South America and the Caribbean.

During a briefing on Tuesday, Liberia’s justice minister, Natu Oswald Tweh, said that the majority of the deportees had committed migration-related violations and offenses, and that they could seek asylum in the west African country if they wished.

The US has agreed to extend visitor visas for Liberians from 12 to 36 months and pledged $124m in assistance as part of the arrangement.

Under a series of often-secret agreements, the Trump administration has deported thousands of people to nearly two dozen countries that are not their own, advocates say, with about 10 of them in Africa. A new report by Refugees International and Human Rights First say the Trump administration has reached deals with at least 35 countries and has sent roughly 23,000 people to 26 of them as of early August, and makes the Liberia agreement the largest single arrangement so far.

Immigration lawyers have said the Trump administration uses deportations to third countries as a legal loophole to indirectly force asylum seekers back to their home countries.

In many cases, migrants are deported to countries they have never been to or where they face safety risks and are left with little choice other than to return to the home countries they were fleeing from.

A February report by Senate foreign relations committee Democrats found the Trump administration had paid more than $32m to five governments, several with poor human rights records, to accept about 300 third-country deportees – including $1.1m per person to Rwanda for seven deportees, and $7.5m to Equatorial Guinea for 29, a sum exceeding all US aid to that country over the previous eight years.

The report found more than 80% of those sent to third countries had since returned home anyway, often at further cost to taxpayers, and cited cases where deportees with US court-ordered protections were removed to Ghana and Equatorial Guinea before being sent onward within days.

The state department disputed the report’s characterization of its enforcement record.

The Associated Press contributed reporting
